'''Florian Cajori''' (February 28, 1859 – August 14<ref name="EB"/><ref>{{Cite journal|title=Florian Cajori 1859-1930|author=Raymond Clare Archibald|journal=Isis|volume=17|number=2|date=January 1932|pages=384–407|doi=10.1086/346660|s2cid=144763935}}</ref> or 15,<ref>Florian Cajori (ed.), [https://books.google.com/books?id=lSoJ2tJKfIEC ''Sir Isaac Newton – Principia'', Vol. 1], University of California Press, 1962, p. ix.</ref> 1930) was a Swiss-American [[historian of mathematics]], especially known for his comprehensive treatise about [[mathematical notation]], ''[[A History of Mathematical Notations]]''.

==Biography==
Florian Cajori was born in [[Zillis-Reischen|Zillis]], [[Switzerland]], as the son of Georg Cajori and Catherine Camenisch.  He attended schools first in Zillis and later in [[Chur]].  In 1875, Florian Cajori emigrated to the United States at the age of sixteen, and attended the [[Wisconsin State College of Milwaukee|State Normal school]] in [[Whitewater, Wisconsin]].  After graduating in 1878, he taught in a country school, and later began studying [[mathematics]] at [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]].<ref name="O'Connor and Robertson" />

In 1883, Cajori received both his bachelor's and master's degrees from the University of Wisconsin–Madison, briefly attended Johns Hopkins University for 8 months in between degrees.<ref>[http://digicoll.library.wisc.edu/cgi-bin/UW/UW-idx?type=div&did=UW.ClassAlbum1883.i0037&isize=M UW Madison class album, 1883]</ref>  He taught for a few years at [[Tulane University]], before being appointed as professor of applied mathematics there in 1887. He was then driven north by tuberculosis.  He founded the Colorado College Scientific Society and taught at [[Colorado College]] where he held the chair in physics from 1889 to 1898 and the chair in mathematics from 1898 to 1918.  He was the position Dean of the engineering department.<ref name="writer">{{cite web|title=Florian Cajori, 1917 MAA President|url=http://www.maa.org/history/presidents/cajori.html|publisher=MAA Mathematical Association of America|access-date=5 July 2012|archive-date=11 February 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120211100228/http://www.maa.org/history/presidents/cajori.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>  While at Colorado, he received his doctorate from Tulane in 1894, and married Elizabeth G. Edwards in 1890 and had one son.<ref name="O'Connor and Robertson" />

Cajori's ''A History of Mathematics'' (1894) was the first popular presentation of the history of mathematics in the United States.<ref name="O'Connor and Robertson">{{cite web|last=O'Connor and Robertson|first=J. J. and E. F.|title=Florian Cajori|url=http://www-history.mcs.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Cajori.html|publisher=The MacTutor History of Mathematics archive, University of S. Andrews, Scotland|access-date=5 July 2012}}</ref>  Based upon his reputation in the history of mathematics (even today his 1928–1929 ''History of Mathematical Notations'' has been described as "unsurpassed")<ref>[http://www2.coloradocollege.edu/dept/ma/history/Faculty/Cajori.html Colorado College page] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101204043525/http://www.coloradocollege.edu/dept/ma/history/Faculty/Cajori.html |date=2010-12-04 }} on Florian Cajori.</ref> he was appointed in 1918 to the first history of mathematics chair in the U.S,  created especially for him, at the [[University of California, Berkeley]]. He remained in Berkeley, California until his death in 1930.  Cajori did no original mathematical research unrelated to the history of mathematics.<ref name="O'Connor and Robertson"/> In addition to his numerous books, he also contributed highly recognized and popular historical articles to the ''[[American Mathematical Monthly]]''.<ref name="writer"/> His last work was a revision of Andrew Motte's 1729 translation of Newton's [[Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica|''Principia'']], vol.1 The Motion of Bodies, but he died before it was completed. The work was finished by R.T. Crawford of Berkeley, California.

==Societies and honors==
* 1917–1918, [[Mathematical Association of America]] president
* 1923, American Association for the Advancement of Science vice-president
* 1924, Invited Speaker of the [[International Congress of Mathematicians]] in 1924 in [[Toronto]]<ref>{{cite book|author=Cajoru, Florian|chapter=Uniformity of mathematical notations—retrospect and prospect|title=''In:'' Proceedings of the International Congress of Mathematicians in Toronto, August 11–16. 1924|volume=2|pages=929–936}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|author=Cajori, Florian|chapter=Past struggles between symbolists and rhetoricians in mathematical publications|title=''In:'' Proceedings of the International Congress of Mathematicians in Toronto, August 11–16. 1924|volume=2|pages=937–942}}</ref>
* 1924–1925, [[History of Science Society]] vice-president
* 1929–1930, Comité International d'Histoire des Sciences vice-president
* The [[Cajori (crater)|Cajori crater]] on the Moon was named in his honour<ref name=GPN>{{gpn|965|Cajori}}</ref>
